messages.content: Our cafe sells beans two ways: a 5 lb bag for $62.00 or a 12 oz bag for $16.50. Which is cheaper per ounce, and by how much?

Convert both to the same unit first: 5 lb is 80 oz.

5 lb bag: $62.00 / 80 oz = $0.775 per oz
12 oz bag: $16.50 / 12 oz = $1.375 per oz

The big bag is cheaper by $1.375 - $0.775 = $0.60 per oz. That gap adds up fast: over 80 oz, the small bags would cost $110.00 against $62.00, a $48.00 difference for the same beans.
Detergent A is 150 oz for $18.99. Detergent B is 100 oz for $13.49. Which is the better buy per ounce?

Divide price by ounces for each:

A: $18.99 / 150 = $0.1266 per oz, about 12.7 cents
B: $13.49 / 100 = $0.1349 per oz, about 13.5 cents

A wins by roughly 0.8 cents per oz. It is a small edge per bottle (about $1.24 over 150 oz), so if B is the one your machine or skin prefers, the premium is modest — but on price alone, A is the better buy.
A salon color tube is 100 ml and costs $9.60. A full-head application uses 60 ml. What does the color product alone cost per appointment, and what is left in the tube worth?

Cost per ml: $9.60 / 100 = $0.096.

Per application: 60 ml x $0.096 = $5.76.

What is left: 40 ml x $0.096 = $3.84 of product remains in the tube.

That $5.76 is the number that belongs in the service's cost column. If the service is priced at $85, product is about 6.8% of the ticket before labor, rent, and everything else.
Paper towels: a 6-roll pack is $7.98 with 60 sheets per roll. A 12-roll pack is $14.28, also 60 sheets per roll. Compare cost per sheet.

Total sheets first:

6-roll pack: 6 x 60 = 360 sheets; $7.98 / 360 = $0.0222 per sheet, about 2.22 cents
12-roll pack: 12 x 60 = 720 sheets; $14.28 / 720 = $0.0198 per sheet, about 1.98 cents

The 12-roll pack saves about 0.23 cents per sheet. On a cafe's usage of, say, 3,600 sheets a year, that is roughly $8.40 a year — real, but small enough that storage space might matter more than the savings.
Protein powder: 2 lb tub, 29 servings, $54.99. Or 5 lb tub, 73 servings, $119.99. Cost per serving for each?

2 lb tub: $54.99 / 29 = $1.896 per serving, so $1.90 rounded to cents.
5 lb tub: $119.99 / 73 = $1.644 per serving, so $1.64.

The big tub saves about $0.25 per serving. At one serving a day that is roughly $92 a year — worth it only if you will actually finish 73 servings before it goes stale, because a tub you abandon at serving 40 was bought at the small-tub outcome with big-tub money.
A standard ink cartridge costs $38 and yields about 400 pages. The XL costs $57 and yields about 750 pages. We print roughly 3,000 pages a year. What do we save with XL?

Cost per page:

Standard: $38 / 400 = $0.095, so 9.5 cents per page
XL: $57 / 750 = $0.076, so 7.6 cents per page

Difference: 1.9 cents per page. Over 3,000 pages: 3,000 x $0.019 = $57.00 saved per year.

One caution: yield ratings assume a standard page coverage. If your pages are dense graphics, both yields drop, but they drop proportionally, so the XL still wins by the same ratio.
A cleaning concentrate is $11.20 for 32 oz and dilutes 1 part concentrate to 8 parts water. The ready-to-use version is $3.84 for 24 oz. Compare the real cost per ounce of usable cleaner.

Dilution is where people undercount. 1:8 means 1 part concentrate plus 8 parts water, so each ounce becomes 9 oz of usable cleaner.

Total usable: 32 x 9 = 288 oz
Concentrate cost: $11.20 / 288 = $0.0389 per oz, about 3.9 cents
Ready-to-use: $3.84 / 24 = $0.16 per oz, exactly 16 cents

The concentrate is about one quarter of the cost per ounce — the ready bottle charges you roughly 4x for the water and the spray bottle. For a business going through gallons, that is the difference between about $5 and about $20.50 per gallon of cleaner.
Eggs: 18-count carton for $4.59 or a dozen for $3.78. Per egg?

18-count: $4.59 / 18 = $0.255 per egg, 25.5 cents.
Dozen: $3.78 / 12 = $0.315 per egg, 31.5 cents.

The 18-count is 6 cents cheaper per egg. If your household uses 3 dozen eggs a week, buying the 18-count saves 36 x $0.06 = $2.16 a week, over $110 a year — as long as they get used before the date on the carton.
Massage oil comes in a 1-gallon jug for $84. I use about 2 oz per session. What is my product cost per session?

A gallon is 128 oz.

Sessions per jug: 128 / 2 = 64 sessions
Cost per session: $84 / 64 = $1.3125, so about $1.31.

That is the consumable cost to build into your session price. If you are charging $70 a session, the oil is under 2% of it — the real costs are your time and the room, not the oil.
Rice: 20 lb bag for $16.40 or 4 lb bag for $4.36. Which is cheaper per pound?

20 lb bag: $16.40 / 20 = $0.82 per lb.
4 lb bag: $4.36 / 4 = $1.09 per lb.

The big bag saves $0.27 per lb — the small bag costs about 33% more per pound. On 20 lb that is $21.80 versus $16.40, a $5.40 difference. Bulk wins here as long as the rice stays dry and gets eaten; rice stores well, so this is one of the safer bulk buys.
Olive oil: a 750 ml bottle at $12.99 versus a 3 liter tin at $41.97. Price per liter for each?

Bottle: $12.99 / 0.75 L = $17.32 per liter.
Tin: $41.97 / 3 L = $13.99 per liter.

The tin saves $3.33 per liter, about 19%. The catch with oil is time: 3 liters is a lot of olive oil, and oil goes rancid. If your kitchen uses a liter a month, the tin is gone in a quarter and the saving is real. If it sits for a year, you saved money on oil you should not eat.
A 30 lb bag of dog food costs $58.99. My dog eats 3 cups a day and there are about 4 cups in a pound. How long does a bag last and what does it cost per day?

arguments.code:
cups = 30 * 4
days = cups / 3
per_day = 58.99 / days
print(cups, days, round(per_day, 4))

messages.content:
Cups in the bag: 30 lb x 4 cups = 120 cups.
Days per bag: 120 / 3 = 40 days.
Daily cost: $58.99 / 40 = $1.4748, so about $1.47 a day.

That is roughly $44.24 a month or $538 a year on food for this dog — the per-day figure is the one to compare when a different brand or bag size catches your eye.
Bottled water: a case of 24 half-liter bottles is $4.80. A filter cartridge is $16 and filters 40 gallons. We drink about 3 gallons a day as a family. Roughly what does each option cost us per year?

First, unit prices.

Bottles: the case holds 24 x 0.5 L = 12 L, which is about 3.17 gallons. $4.80 / 3.17 = about $1.51 per gallon.
Filter: $16 / 40 gallons = $0.40 per gallon.

Annual use: 3 gal/day x 365 = 1,095 gallons.

Bottles: 1,095 x $1.51 = about $1,653 per year.
Filter: 1,095 x $0.40 = $438 per year (that is about 27 cartridges).

Difference: roughly $1,215 a year. The bottled habit costs nearly four times the filtered one — and that is before counting the trips to the store.
Backbar shampoo is $46 for a 1 liter bottle. Each wash uses about 15 ml. Cost per wash?

Washes per bottle: 1,000 ml / 15 ml = 66.7, so 66 full washes with a little left over.

Cost per wash: $46 / 66.7 = $0.69.

Call it 69 cents of shampoo per wash. If the salon does 40 washes a day, that is about $27.60 a day in shampoo — small per wash, but it is exactly the kind of line that belongs in the per-service cost, because it never stops.
Napkins for the shop: 500-pack for $6.25 or 250-pack for $3.75. We need 2,000. What do we pay each way?

Per napkin:
500-pack: $6.25 / 500 = 1.25 cents
250-pack: $3.75 / 250 = 1.5 cents

For 2,000 napkins:
Four 500-packs: 4 x $6.25 = $25.00
Eight 250-packs: 8 x $3.75 = $30.00

The bigger pack saves $5.00 on this order, 17% less. Napkins do not expire, so this is a pure win if you have the shelf space.
A jacket is $84, marked 25% off, and sales tax here is 7%. What do I actually pay? A friend says to add tax first, then discount. Who is right?

Discount first, because tax is charged on the price you actually pay:

Discounted price: $84 x 0.75 = $63.00
Tax: $63.00 x 7% = $4.41
You pay: $63.00 + $4.41 = $67.41.

Fun fact for your friend: mathematically the order does not change the total — $84 x 1.07 x 0.75 is also $67.41, because multiplication commutes. But the receipt is written discount-first, and the register computes tax on $63. Either road arrives at $67.41.
My savings rate went from 4% to 5%. The bank's email says rates rose 1%. My coworker says they rose 25%. One of them has to be wrong, right?

Both are describing the same move with different yardsticks, and the bank's phrasing is the slippery one.

Percentage points: 5% - 4% = 1 percentage point. That is the honest unit for the change in a rate.
Percent change: the increase of 1 point relative to where you started, 1 / 4 = 25%. Your coworker is right in relative terms.

So 'rates rose 1%' is wrong — rates rose 1 percentage point, which is a 25% increase. On $10,000, the practical difference: $400 a year at 4% versus $500 at 5%. Whenever someone quotes a change in a percentage, ask: points, or percent of the old value?
After a 20% price increase, my software subscription costs $96 a month. What was it before? I keep wanting to just take 20% off 96.

Resist that urge — it is the most common percentage mistake there is.

The $96 is 120% of the old price, so divide by 1.20:

$96 / 1.20 = $80.00.

Check: $80 x 1.20 = $96. Correct.

Why your instinct fails: 20% of $96 is $19.20, and $96 - $19.20 = $76.80. But the increase was 20% of the OLD price ($16 on $80), not 20% of the new one. Percentages always belong to a base, and the base here is the price before the increase. To undo any percent increase, divide by (1 + rate); never subtract the percent from the final number.
My rent went up 8% and is now $1,458. What was I paying before the increase?

The new rent is 108% of the old rent:

$1,458 / 1.08 = $1,350.00.

Check: $1,350 x 1.08 = $1,458. Exactly right.

Note the increase itself was $108, which is 8% of $1,350 — not 8% of $1,458 (that would be $116.64). Reverse percentages always divide by the growth factor; they never subtract a percent of the final amount.

Three of us had dinner. Our food cost $22, $31, and $18. Tax and tip together add 25% on top. Splitting evenly feels wrong since we ordered differently. What does each person owe if we split proportionally?

Proportional split: apply the same 25% uplift to each person's own food, so everyone pays their share of tax and tip in proportion to what they ordered.

Person 1: $22 x 1.25 = $27.50
Person 2: $31 x 1.25 = $38.75
Person 3: $18 x 1.25 = $22.50

Total check: $27.50 + $38.75 + $22.50 = $88.75, which matches the bill: ($22 + $31 + $18) x 1.25 = $71 x 1.25 = $88.75.

An even split would be $29.58 each — the $18 eater would subsidize the $31 eater by about $7. Proportional is the fair method whenever the orders differ by more than a few dollars.
Dinner subtotal was $64 and tax is 8.5%. I tip 20%. Does it matter whether I tip on the subtotal or on the after-tax total?

It matters by about a dollar here, and more on bigger checks.

After-tax total: $64 x 1.085 = $69.44.
Tip on subtotal (the traditional base): $64 x 20% = $12.80.
Tip on after-tax total: $69.44 x 20% = $13.89 (rounded).

Difference: about $1.09.

The convention is tipping on the pre-tax subtotal — you are tipping on the food and service, not on the government's cut. Card readers that suggest tip percentages on the post-tax total quietly raise every suggested tip by the tax rate. Knowing the base lets you choose on purpose.
I take home $2,850 a month and my rent is $975. What percentage of my income is rent?

$975 / $2,850 = 0.3421, so about 34.2% of your take-home pay.

Context: the old rule of thumb says keep housing at or under 30% of gross pay. You are at 34.2% of take-home, which is tighter than the guideline but not unusual in current rental markets. The useful number for your own budgeting is the one you just computed — percent of money you actually receive — because that is the money that has to cover everything else too.
A blender was $129.99 and I bought it for $84.49. The sign said 35% off. Was the sign right?

Amount saved: $129.99 - $84.49 = $45.50.
As a percent of the original price: $45.50 / $129.99 = 35.003%.

The sign was right: 35% off, to within a rounding whisker. The discount percent is always measured against the original price — measure it against the sale price and you would get 53.9%, which is the trap answer the sign is not claiming.
I earn 7.5% commission on my sales. Last month I sold $18,400 worth. What is my commission?

$18,400 x 0.075 = $1,380.00.

Quick sanity check: 10% of $18,400 would be $1,840, and 7.5% is three quarters of that, and three quarters of $1,840 is $1,380. Matches. Estimating a nearby round percent first is a good habit — it catches decimal-point slips before they reach your paycheck math.
I paid $53.50 total for a repair part and the tax rate is 7%. What was the price before tax?

The $53.50 is 107% of the pre-tax price:

$53.50 / 1.07 = $50.00.

Check: $50.00 x 0.07 = $3.50 tax; $50.00 + $3.50 = $53.50. Exact.

Do not compute 7% of $53.50 and subtract — that gives $49.76, which is wrong, because the tax was 7% of the smaller pre-tax amount, not 7% of the total.
Four of us are splitting a $137.60 dinner bill evenly, with an 18% tip on top. What does each person pay?

Tip: $137.60 x 18% = $24.768, so $24.77 rounded to cents.
Total with tip: $137.60 + $24.77 = $162.37.
Per person: $162.37 / 4 = $40.5925, so $40.59 each.

Four payments of $40.59 total $162.36 — one cent short, because the exact share is $40.5925. Someone tosses in the extra penny and the table is settled.
Our fundraiser goal is $12,000 and we have raised $9,300. What percent are we at, and how much is left?

$9,300 / $12,000 = 0.775, so you are at 77.5% of goal.

Remaining: $12,000 - $9,300 = $2,700, which is the other 22.5%.

A useful framing for the final push: you need to raise 29% of what you have already raised ($2,700 / $9,300), not 29% of the goal — donors respond better to 'we are 77.5% there' anyway.
My employer cut my pay 10% last year. This year they promise a raise that 'restores' it. They offered 10%. Is that actually a restoration?

No — a 10% raise on the reduced pay does not get you back. Run it on $1,000 for clarity:

After the cut: $1,000 x 0.90 = $900.
After a 10% raise on $900: $900 x 1.10 = $990.

You are still $10 short, because the raise is 10% of the smaller base. To fully restore $900 to $1,000 you need $1,000 / $900 = 1.1111, an 11.11% raise.

The general rule: a cut of X% always needs a raise of more than X% to undo it, because the raise applies to less money. A 10% cut needs 11.11%; a 20% cut needs 25%; a 50% cut needs 100%.
A class pass dropped from $45 to $36 and my friend called it a 20% drop. Now it is going back up to $45. Is that a 20% increase?

Your friend is right about the drop: ($45 - $36) / $45 = $9 / $45 = 20%.

But the trip back is not 20%: ($45 - $36) / $36 = $9 / $36 = 25%.

Same $9, different base. Going down, the $9 is measured against $45; going up, against $36. Percent changes are not symmetric — a 20% fall always needs a 25% rise to undo it. This is why 'down 20%, then up 20%' never lands you back where you started.
A store raised a chair's price from $80 to $100, then put it on sale at '25% off.' My sister says that just puts it back to $80. Is she right?

She is not, and this is the base trap in a trench coat.

The raise: $80 to $100 is +25%.
The sale: 25% off $100 = $100 x 0.75 = $75.

The sale price is $75, not $80. The 25% discount is taken from the higher $100 price, so it removes $25, while the original markup only added $20. Net effect versus the original price: $75 / $80 = 0.9375 — the chair is actually 6.25% cheaper than before the whole dance. 'Up 25%, down 25%' always ends below the start.
I have exactly $200 to spend on a tool, tax included. Tax is 8.25%. What is the highest sticker price I can afford?

The sticker price plus 8.25% tax must equal $200 at most:

Sticker x 1.0825 = $200
Sticker = $200 / 1.0825 = $184.76 (rounded to cents).

Check: $184.76 x 0.0825 = $15.24 tax; $184.76 + $15.24 = $200.00. Right at the line.

The common error is subtracting 8.25% of $200 ($16.50) and shopping for a $183.50 tool — that leaves money on the table, because tax is computed on the sticker, not on your $200.
We have 250 employees. 30% work part-time, and 40% of the part-timers are students. How many student part-timers do we have?

Percent of a percent multiplies:

Part-timers: 250 x 30% = 75 people.
Students among them: 75 x 40% = 30 people.

Or in one step: 0.30 x 0.40 = 0.12, so 12% of all employees are student part-timers, and 250 x 0.12 = 30.

Never add the percents (30% + 40% = 70% would claim 175 people). When a percent applies to a subgroup, it multiplies against the whole.
The restaurant added an automatic 20% gratuity to our party's $86 check. I wanted to tip a little extra, about 5%. What will my total tip be, in dollars and as a percent?

Automatic gratuity: $86 x 20% = $17.20.
Your extra 5% (of the same $86 check): $86 x 5% = $4.30.
Total tip: $17.20 + $4.30 = $21.50.

As a percent: $21.50 / $86 = 25%. Since both percents are taken from the same base — the $86 check — they simply add: 20% + 5% = 25%. Percents add cleanly only when they share a base; that is the exception people wrongly assume is the rule.
I lend a friend $5,000 at 4.5% simple interest for 3 years. How much interest do I earn, and what do I get back?

Simple interest: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time.

$5,000 x 0.045 x 3 = $675.00 interest.
Total back: $5,000 + $675 = $5,675.00.

Simple interest is computed only on the original $5,000 every year — $225 a year, three times. It is the friendliest possible structure for the borrower, which is worth knowing before you agree to it: a bank would compound, and compounding pays the lender more.
Same deal as simple interest — $5,000 at 4.5% for 3 years — but compounded annually. How much more does compounding pay?

Compound growth: $5,000 x 1.045^3 = $5,705.83 (rounded to cents).

Interest earned: $705.83.
Simple interest on the same terms pays $675.00.
Compounding pays $30.83 more.

That $30.83 is interest on interest: year one's $225 itself earns 4.5% in years two and three. Over 3 years at 4.5% the effect is small; stretch it to 30 years and compounding stops being a footnote and becomes the whole story.
A bank offers 6% on $10,000 for one year. Does it matter if interest compounds annually or monthly?

Annually: $10,000 x 1.06 = $10,600. Interest: $600.00.

Monthly: each month you earn 6% / 12 = 0.5%, and it compounds: $10,000 x 1.005^12 = $10,616.78. Interest: $616.78.

Difference: $16.78 in your favor with monthly compounding.

That is why banks quote APY (annual percentage yield) for deposits: the 6% compounded monthly is really a 6.17% APY. Whenever you compare accounts, compare APY to APY — the compounding frequency is baked into it.
I am financing a car: $18,000 loan, 6.9% APR, 60 months. What is the monthly payment and the total interest? Show me the formula actually working.

arguments.code:
P, annual, n = 18000, 0.069, 60
r = annual / 12
pmt = round(P * r / (1 - (1 + r) ** -n), 2)
print(pmt, round(pmt * n, 2), round(pmt * n - P, 2))

messages.content:
The amortizing payment formula is PMT = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n), where r is the monthly rate.

r = 6.9% / 12 = 0.575% per month, n = 60.
Monthly payment: $355.57.
Total paid: $355.57 x 60 = $21,334.20.
Total interest: $21,334.20 - $18,000 = $3,334.20.

So the car costs you $3,334.20 in interest — about 18.5% on top of the amount borrowed. That total-interest figure, not the monthly payment, is the number to compare when a dealer offers you a longer term with a 'lower payment.'
What would the monthly payment be on a $240,000 mortgage at 6.5% for 30 years? Principal and interest only.

arguments.code:
P, annual, n = 240000, 0.065, 360
r = annual / 12
pmt = round(P * r / (1 - (1 + r) ** -n), 2)
print(pmt, round(pmt * n, 2), round(pmt * n - P, 2))

messages.content:
Monthly rate r = 6.5% / 12 = 0.5417%, n = 360 payments.

Payment: $1,516.96 per month.
Total paid over 30 years: $1,516.96 x 360 = $546,105.60.
Total interest: $546,105.60 - $240,000 = $306,105.60.

Read that again: the interest exceeds the amount borrowed. At 6.5% over 30 years you buy the house and then buy it again for the bank. This is why the rate and the term matter more than any other two numbers in the deal — and why extra principal payments early, when the balance is highest, do outsized damage to that $306k.
I owe $9,500 on a loan at 3% annual interest. I can pay $300 a month, or stretch to $400. How much sooner am I done at $400, and how much interest do I save?

With monthly rate r = 3% / 12 = 0.25%, the months to pay off are n = -ln(1 - rP/A) / ln(1 + r), where A is the payment.

At $300/month: n is about 33.0 months. Total paid about $9,910, so interest is about $410.
At $400/month: n is about 24.5 months. Total paid about $9,806, so interest is about $306.

The extra $100 a month finishes the loan roughly 8.5 months sooner and saves about $104 in interest.

At 3% the interest saving is modest — the real prize is being done sooner. At credit-card rates the same $100 would save several times more interest, which is why extra payments should always hunt the highest rate first.
People say money earning 8% doubles in about 9 years. Is that actually true?

Check it directly: $1 growing at 8% for 9 years becomes 1.08^9 = $1.999 — within a tenth of a cent of exactly $2.

So yes, it is true, and it is not a coincidence. The Rule of 72 says doubling time in years is about 72 divided by the rate: 72 / 8 = 9 years. The rule works because ln(2) is about 0.693 and the math of small rates rounds kindly to 72.

Use it as a mental shortcut anywhere: at 6% money doubles in about 12 years; at 9%, about 8 years; at 12%, about 6 years.
One account advertises 5% APR compounded monthly, another just says 5% APY. Are they the same on $20,000 for a year?

Not the same. APR with monthly compounding earns more than the headline 5%:

Effective yield = (1 + 0.05/12)^12 - 1 = 5.116%.

On $20,000 for one year:
5% APR compounded monthly: $20,000 x 1.05116 = $21,023.24 (about $1,023.24 interest).
5% APY flat: $20,000 x 1.05 = $21,000.00 ($1,000 interest).

Difference: about $23.24 in favor of the APR account. APY is the honest, comparable number — it already includes compounding. When one offer quotes APR and another APY, convert the APR to its effective yield before deciding, or you are comparing a dressed-up number to a plain one.
A lender offers me a $150,000 interest-only loan at 5%. Payments sound low. What am I actually paying, and what do I owe at the end of 5 years?

Interest-only payment: $150,000 x 5% / 12 = $625.00 per month.

Over 5 years: $625 x 60 = $37,500 paid.
Balance at the end: still $150,000. Every cent of the $37,500 was interest; the principal never moved.

Compare an amortizing loan: the payment would be higher, but part of every payment retires principal, so the balance — and the interest charged on it — shrinks monthly. Interest-only is a tool for short, planned situations (a flip, a bridge). As a long-term home for a debt, it is renting money.
I put $20,000 in an 18-month CD at 4.2%. How much interest do I earn?

The quick estimate, treating it as simple interest:

$20,000 x 0.042 x 1.5 years = $1,260.00.

Most CDs actually compound, typically semiannually or quarterly. Compounded semiannually: $20,000 x (1 + 0.042/2)^3 = $20,000 x 1.021^3 = $21,286.65, so interest of $1,286.65.

So expect between $1,260 and about $1,287 depending on the compounding schedule in the fine print — a $27 difference that tells you whether the bank's marketing number was the simple or the honest one. Either way, you walk away with roughly $21,260 to $21,287 at maturity.
Personal loan quote: $7,500 at 9% for 36 months. Payment and total interest?

arguments.code:
P, annual, n = 7500, 0.09, 36
r = annual / 12
pmt = P * r / (1 - (1 + r) ** -n)
print(round(pmt, 2))

messages.content:
Monthly rate r = 9% / 12 = 0.75%, n = 36.

Monthly payment: $238.50.
Total paid: $238.50 x 36 = $8,586.00.
Total interest: $8,586.00 - $7,500 = $1,086.00.

Interest is about 14.5% of the amount borrowed over the three years. If a lender quotes you the same loan as '$238 a month' without the totals, do this multiplication yourself — the total interest is the price of the loan, and it is the only fair basis for comparing offers.
A payday place charges $15 per $100 borrowed, due in two weeks. That sounds small. What is the actual annual rate?

Convert the fee to a rate, then annualize it.

Fee rate for two weeks: $15 / $100 = 15%.
Periods in a year: 52 weeks / 2 = 26.
APR = 15% x 26 = 390%.

Borrow $300 and the fee is $45 for two weeks. Roll it over — which is where the model makes its money — and three rollovers cost $180 in fees on a $300 loan that you still owe in full.

'Fifteen dollars' sounds small because the period is short. Any fee quoted per week or per two weeks should be multiplied out to a year before you judge it; that is the comparison the storefront is hoping you skip.
I need $6,000 in 15 months for a certification course. A savings account pays 0.3% per month. How much do I need to deposit monthly?

The sinking-fund formula: PMT = FV x r / ((1 + r)^n - 1).

PMT = $6,000 x 0.003 / (1.003^15 - 1) = $391.67 per month (rounded to cents).

Check: 15 deposits of $391.67 total $5,875.05 out of pocket, and the account's interest contributes the remaining roughly $124.95 to reach $6,000.

Without interest you would need exactly $400 a month. The interest only saves you about $8.33 a month here — at small rates and short horizons, the deposit does nearly all the work. Time in the market is what makes interest matter, and 15 months is not much time.
If inflation runs 3% a year, what will $1,000 under the mattress actually buy in 10 years?

Money under the mattress stays $1,000 nominally, but its purchasing power divides by the inflation factor:

$1,000 / 1.03^10 = $1,000 / 1.3439 = $744.09 of today's buying power.

So a decade of 3% inflation quietly takes about $256 — a quarter of the value — from cash that 'didn't lose anything.'

This is the real baseline for any savings decision: an account paying less than inflation is still losing ground, just more slowly and with better marketing. Cash has a return too; it is negative.
Two offers for a $10,000 loan: 7% for 3 years, or 5.5% for 5 years. The 5.5% has the lower rate AND the lower payment. It has to be cheaper, right?

Wrong — and this is the most expensive intuition in consumer lending.

7% for 3 years: payment $308.77, total interest $1,115.75.
5.5% for 5 years: payment $191.01, total interest $1,460.70.

The 'cheaper' loan costs $344.95 MORE in interest. The lower rate loses to the longer term: you pay interest on the balance for 24 extra months, and time beats rate here.

Rate, term, and total interest are three different numbers. Lenders advertise the first two because the third is the one that tells you what the loan costs.
I have a $2,400 credit card balance at 24% APR. If I just pay $60 a month flat, how long until it is gone and how much interest do I pay?

Monthly rate r = 24% / 12 = 2%. First check the payment even works: interest in month one is $2,400 x 2% = $48, so $60 clears it by only $12 — slow but survivable.

Months to pay off: n = -ln(1 - rP/A) / ln(1 + r) = -ln(1 - 48/60) / ln(1.02) = -ln(0.2) / ln(1.02), which is about 81.3 months — nearly 6 years and 10 months.

Total paid: about 81.3 x $60 = $4,876. Interest: roughly $2,476 — more than the original balance.

And notice the cliff edge: at $48 a month you would pay forever and owe exactly $2,400 at the end of every month. Minimum-payment structures are engineered to live just above that line.
Refinancing my mortgage would drop my payment from $1,486 to $1,392, but closing costs are $2,850. How long until the refinance actually pays off?

Monthly saving: $1,486 - $1,392 = $94.
Break-even: $2,850 / $94 = 30.3 months, so 31 months — about 2 years and 7 months — before the savings repay the closing costs.

Before month 31, the refinance has cost you money. After it, you keep $94 a month.

So the decision is really a bet on staying: if you expect to sell or refinance again within about two and a half years, keep the current loan. One more wrinkle: if the new loan restarts a 30-year clock, compare total interest too — a lower payment bought by stretching the term can cost more overall even after the break-even point.
I have $8,000 to park for 2 years. One bank pays 4.4% APY, another 3.9% APY, both compounded annually. How much does the half-point difference actually come to?

4.4% account: $8,000 x 1.044^2 = $8,000 x 1.089936 = $8,719.49.
3.9% account: $8,000 x 1.039^2 = $8,000 x 1.079521 = $8,636.17.

Difference: $8,719.49 - $8,636.17 = $83.32 over the two years.

Half a percentage point sounds trivial and is — on $8,000 over 2 years. Scale it to $80,000 over 10 years and the same gap is worth thousands. Rate differences matter in proportion to principal times time; always multiply before deciding whether to bother switching.
Shop revenue was $42,300 in March and $45,711 in April. What is the month-over-month growth?

Change: $45,711 - $42,300 = $3,411.
Growth: $3,411 / $42,300 = 0.0806, so +8.06% month over month.

Always divide by the earlier month — the base is where you started. And one caution before celebrating: a single month-over-month jump says little. April could have one more weekend than March. Compare against last April too before calling it a trend.
My side business did $80,000 four years ago and $121,000 this year. What was the compound annual growth rate over those four years?

CAGR = (final / start)^(1/years) - 1 = (121,000 / 80,000)^(1/4) - 1 = 1.5125^0.25 - 1 = 0.1090, so about 10.90% per year.

Check: $80,000 x 1.109^4 = about $121,000. Right.

CAGR is the smoothed rate — the steady annual growth that would connect the two endpoints. The actual years were surely bumpier; CAGR hides the path on purpose, which makes it good for comparisons and bad for storytelling. One warning: the exponent is the number of years between the figures, so if that $80,000 were three years old instead of four, the same endpoints would mean a much stronger 14.8% CAGR.
Our gym went from 640 members to 512 over exactly one year, declining steadily. What is the average monthly decline rate?

Total change: 512 / 640 = 0.80, a 20% loss over the year.

Monthly rate: 0.80^(1/12) - 1 = -1.84% per month.

Verified: 640 x (1 - 0.0184)^12 lands back on 512.

Note that -20% divided by 12 would give -1.67% a month, which understates it — dividing a total percent by the number of periods ignores compounding. At -1.84% a month, if nothing changes, the gym crosses below 410 members within another year. That is the number to act on.
Our user base grows 12% a year. How long until it doubles? And how close is it after just 6 years?

Exact doubling time: ln(2) / ln(1.12) = 6.12 years.

After 6 years: 1.12^6 = 1.9738, so the base has grown by 97.4% — just shy of doubled, which matches the 6.12-year answer.

The Rule of 72 estimate: 72 / 12 = 6 years. Close enough for planning, and the exact computation shows the rule errs slightly optimistically at this rate. A base of 5,000 users becomes about 9,869 in 6 years and crosses 10,000 a couple of months later.
My portfolio went up 10% last quarter and down 10% this quarter. So I am back where I started, right?

Not quite — you are down 1%. Take $250 as the example:

Up 10%: $250 x 1.10 = $275.
Down 10%: $275 x 0.90 = $247.50.

Net: $247.50 / $250 = 0.99, a 1% loss.

The 10% decline applied to more money ($275) than the 10% gain did ($250), so it removed $27.50 while the gain added $25. Equal and opposite percents never cancel; the product 1.10 x 0.90 = 0.99 tells the true story every time.
A town of 18,400 people is growing 2.5% a year. What is the population in 5 years if the rate holds?

Compound it year on year: $18,400 x 1.025^5 = 20,817.91, so about 20,818 people.

Growth added: about 2,418 people. Simple (non-compounding) growth would give 18,400 x (1 + 5 x 0.025) = 20,700 — the compounding adds an extra 118 because each year's new residents are themselves part of next year's base.

Five years is short enough that the two methods nearly agree; over 25 years they would diverge by thousands.
My blog traffic is falling 15% a month. I am at 10,000 visits. Where am I in 4 months at this rate?

Each month keeps 85% of the previous month:

10,000 x 0.85^4 = 10,000 x 0.5220 = 5,220 visits (rounded).

So a steady 15% monthly decline cuts traffic nearly in half in four months — the halfway point is about month 4.3, since 0.85^4.3 is about 0.50.

Declines compound just like growth does, only downward. And note the asymmetry: to climb back from 5,220 to 10,000 you would need +91.6% total growth, not +47.8%. Losses dig a hole that equal-percent gains cannot refill.
I want my savings to double in 7 years. What annual growth rate do I need?

Solve (1 + r)^7 = 2:

r = 2^(1/7) - 1 = 0.1041, so about 10.41% per year.

Rule of 72 check: 72 / 7 = 10.29% — close, slightly under the exact 10.41%.

Context: 10.4% a year for seven straight years is an ambitious target — above long-run stock market averages and far above any savings account. If the goal is firm, either the timeline stretches (at 7% it takes about 10.2 years) or contributions have to do part of the work that growth cannot.
First quarter last year we billed $212,000. This first quarter: $244,000. Year-over-year growth?

Change: $244,000 - $212,000 = $32,000.
Growth: $32,000 / $212,000 = 0.1509, so +15.09% year over year.

Year-over-year is the comparison that matters for a seasonal business — it matches like periods against like, so the +15.09% is real growth rather than a calendar artifact. Both numbers belong in the report: the $32,000 is what you can spend; the 15.09% is how you judge the trajectory.
We sell 950 units a month. Plan A assumes we add a flat 40 units a month. Plan B assumes 4% monthly growth. Which plan is bigger after 6 months?

Plan A (linear): 950 + 6 x 40 = 950 + 240 = 1,190 units.

Plan B (compound): 950 x 1.04^6 = 950 x 1.26532 = 1,202 units (rounded).

Plan B wins after 6 months, by about 12 units — and the gap widens every month after, because Plan B's monthly addition grows (38 units the first month, 46 by the sixth) while Plan A adds the same 40 forever.

Early on, though, Plan A was ahead: in month one it added 40 against Plan B's 38. Linear plans sprint, compound plans marathon. Which forecast to trust depends on what actually drives your sales — capacity you add in fixed steps, or a base that grows itself.
Revenue grew 18% in 2024 and 12% in 2025. My partner says that is 30% total growth over the two years. Correct him.

Growth rates multiply; they do not add.

Start with $100 for clarity:
After 2024: $100 x 1.18 = $118.
After 2025: $118 x 1.12 = $132.16.

Total growth: 32.16%, not 30%.

The missing 2.16 points are the second year's 12% acting on the first year's gains: 12% of the extra $18 is $2.16. Your partner's addition would be right only if both percents were measured against the original base — but the 2025 growth grew from the bigger 2024 number. (This is also why two years of losses are worse than they look when added: the multiplication cuts both ways.)
My gym kept membership at $70 but quietly cut sessions from 60 minutes to 50. A member says that is a price increase in disguise. How big, exactly?

Price per minute, before: $70 / 60 = $1.1667 per minute.
Price per minute, after: $70 / 50 = $1.40 per minute.
Increase: ($1.40 - $1.1667) / $1.1667 = 0.20, exactly 20%.

The member is right, and it is a 20% effective increase — steeper than most gyms would dare post on the door. Shrinkflation works by holding the sticker constant and shrinking the unit, which is why the honest comparison is always price per unit: per minute here, per ounce at the grocery store. The sticker is the one number they want you to watch; the unit price is the one that tells the truth.
I buy a product for $60 and sell it for $100. A supplier rep called that a 40% markup. My accountant calls it a 40% margin. Who is using the words right?

Your accountant.

Margin is profit as a share of the selling price: ($100 - $60) / $100 = 40%.
Markup is profit as a share of the cost: ($100 - $60) / $60 = 66.7%.

Same $40 of profit, two different denominators. Margin can never exceed 100%; markup happily can (a $10 item sold for $30 is a 200% markup but a 66.7% margin).

This confusion is expensive in both directions: price using '40% markup' when you meant 40% margin and you underprice; report a 66.7% markup as if it were margin and you overstate profitability. Always ask: percent of what — cost, or price?
A candle costs me $34 to make. I want a 45% gross margin. What price do I set?

Price from a target margin: Price = Cost / (1 - margin).

$34 / (1 - 0.45) = $34 / 0.55 = $61.82 (rounded to cents).

Check: profit is $61.82 - $34 = $27.82, and $27.82 / $61.82 = 45.0%. Correct.

The tempting shortcut — add 45% to cost — gives $34 x 1.45 = $49.30, whose margin is only ($49.30 - $34) / $49.30 = 31%. Marking up by the margin percent is the single most common pricing error in small business; dividing by (1 - margin) is the fix.
I mark a $27.50 item up by 80%. What is the selling price, and what margin does that give me?

Selling price: $27.50 x 1.80 = $49.50.
Profit: $49.50 - $27.50 = $22.00.
Margin: $22.00 / $49.50 = 44.4%.

So an 80% markup is a 44.4% margin — the two numbers are never equal except at zero. The conversion, if you need it often: margin = markup / (1 + markup). Here 0.80 / 1.80 = 0.4444. An 80% markup sounds like you keep most of the price; in truth you keep 44 cents of each dollar and the other 56 cents replaces the product.
My food truck has $4,800 a month in fixed costs. Each meal sells for $45 and costs $21 in ingredients and packaging. How many meals a month to break even?

Contribution per meal: $45 - $21 = $24. That $24 is what each sale contributes toward fixed costs.

Break-even: $4,800 / $24 = 200 meals per month.

At 200 meals you cover exactly the $4,800 — profit zero, not a dollar earned. Meal 201 is the first one that makes money. Over a 26-day month that is about 7.7 meals a day just to stand still, which is the number to hold in your head on a slow Tuesday.
A salon's fixed monthly costs are $9,350. A service is priced at $120 and uses $55 of product and direct labor. How many of those services a month to break even?

Contribution per service: $120 - $55 = $65.
Break-even: $9,350 / $65 = 143.85 services.

You cannot sell 0.85 of a service, so round UP: 144 services a month. At 143 you are $55 short of covering fixed costs; at 144 you are $10 ahead.

Break-even counts always round up — rounding down or to nearest quietly plans a small loss. Across six stylists, 144 services is 24 each per month, which turns an abstract target into a per-person one.
A product sells for $80 and costs $52, so a 35% margin. I am thinking of a 15%-off sale. What happens to the margin?

Sale price: $80 x 0.85 = $68.
New profit: $68 - $52 = $16.
New margin: $16 / $68 = 23.5%.

So a 15% price cut took the margin from 35% to 23.5% — the margin fell by nearly a third, because the entire discount comes out of the profit slice; the $52 cost does not discount itself.

Volume math: at $28 profit per unit before, versus $16 now, you must sell $28 / $16 = 1.75x as many units — 75% more — just to make the same total profit. Most sales never clear that bar; run this division before the sale, not after.
I expect to sell about 500 units. Fixed costs are $6,000 and each unit costs me $18 to make. What price breaks even at 500 units?

The price must cover the unit cost plus each unit's share of fixed costs:

Fixed cost per unit: $6,000 / 500 = $12.
Break-even price: $18 + $12 = $30.00.

Check: 500 x $30 = $15,000 revenue; costs are $6,000 + 500 x $18 = $15,000. Exactly even.

Notice the trap inside the formula: the $30 is only break-even IF you sell all 500. Sell 400 at $30 and you take in $12,000 against $13,200 of costs — a $1,200 loss. Break-even price depends on a volume guess, so price for the volume you are confident of, not the volume you hope for.
Last month we sold 340 units at $29 each. Each unit cost $17.40. What was the gross profit?

Profit per unit: $29.00 - $17.40 = $11.60.
Gross profit: 340 x $11.60 = $3,944.00.

For reference: revenue was 340 x $29 = $9,860, and the gross margin is $3,944 / $9,860 = 40%. Gross profit is before rent, wages, and the rest of overhead — it is the pool those bills get paid from, not the money you made.
I sell a service online for $120. The platform takes 8%, and my cost to deliver is $64. What is my real profit and margin per sale?

Platform fee: $120 x 8% = $9.60.
What you keep from the price: $120 - $9.60 = $110.40.
Profit: $110.40 - $64 = $46.40.
Margin: $46.40 / $120 = 38.7%.

The fee comes off the top, before your costs, so it behaves like a price cut you never see. If you had computed margin ignoring the fee you would have said ($120 - $64) / $120 = 46.7% — eight points of fiction. Fees calculated on the gross price always belong inside the margin math, not underneath it.
A wholesaler sells me a jacket for $42. I mark it up 55%. Then it goes on sale at 20% off. What does the customer pay, and am I still making money?

Your price: $42 x 1.55 = $65.10.
Sale price: $65.10 x 0.80 = $52.08.
Profit at the sale price: $52.08 - $42 = $10.08.
Margin on the sale: $10.08 / $52.08 = 19.4%.

Yes, still profitable — the 55% markup built in enough cushion that a 20% discount leaves a 19.4% margin. This is exactly why retailers mark up generously before sale season: the discount is taken from the marked-up price, not from cost. The break point for this jacket would be a discount of about 35.5% — beyond that, you are paying customers to take it.
I sell through a marketplace that takes 5% of the price. My cost is $50 and I want a true 30% margin AFTER the fee. What price do I need?

Set it up as: Price - fee - cost = margin x Price. The fee takes 5% of price and the margin must be 30% of price, so cost is what remains:

Price = $50 / (1 - 0.05 - 0.30) = $50 / 0.65 = $76.92 (rounded to cents).

Verify: fee is $76.92 x 5% = $3.85. Profit: $76.92 - $3.85 - $50 = $23.07. Margin: $23.07 / $76.92 = 30.0%. Exact.

If you had priced for margin while ignoring the fee — $50 / 0.70 = $71.43 — the fee would quietly eat $3.57 and your true margin would land at 25%, not 30%. Any percent-of-price charge has to be inside the divisor.
My shop sells two products in a steady 3-to-1 ratio. Product A: $40 price, 50% margin. Product B: $90 price, 20% margin. What is my blended margin?

Work in a representative basket of 4 units — 3 of A, 1 of B:

Revenue: 3 x $40 + 1 x $90 = $120 + $90 = $210.
Profit: 3 x ($40 x 50%) + 1 x ($90 x 20%) = 3 x $20 + $18 = $78.
Blended margin: $78 / $210 = 37.1%.

Note it is not the average of 50% and 20% (that would be 35%), because the blend is weighted by dollars, not by products. B is only a quarter of the units but 43% of the revenue, so its weak margin drags harder than the unit count suggests. If you want to lift the blend, pushing B's margin or price moves it more than selling one extra A.
My candle costs $8 and sells for $20, and I sell 200 a month. If I raise the price to $22 but sales drop to 170, am I better off?

Before: margin is ($20 - $8) / $20 = 60%. Profit: 200 x $12 = $2,400 a month.
After: profit per candle is $22 - $8 = $14, and margin rises to $14 / $22 = 63.6%. But profit: 170 x $14 = $2,380 a month.

You are $20 a month WORSE off, despite a higher price and a prettier margin percent.

Margin percent is a ratio; profit is money. The raise needed volume to stay above $2,400 / $14 = 171.4, so 172 candles, to pay off. At 170 it just misses. Whenever a price change trades margin against volume, multiply it out — the ratio will flatter the decision every time.
Two services compete for the same chair time. Service A: $90 price, $30 variable cost, takes 1 hour. Service B: $150 price, $60 variable cost, takes 2 hours. Which should I promote?

Compare contribution per hour, because the chair is the scarce resource:

A: ($90 - $30) / 1 hr = $60 per hour.
B: ($150 - $60) / 2 hr = $45 per hour.

Promote A. B has the bigger ticket and the bigger per-service profit ($90 vs $60), but it occupies the chair twice as long. In a 6-hour day, A yields 6 x $60 = $360 of contribution; B yields 3 x $90 = $270.

Whenever two offers compete for the same limited resource — chair hours, oven space, a delivery van — rank them by contribution per unit of that resource, never by ticket size.
My fixed costs are $3,600 a month and each unit contributes $28. But if I sell more than 150 units I have to hire help for another $900 a month. Where are my break-even points?

There are two, and a dead zone between them.

Without the hire: $3,600 / $28 = 128.6, so break-even at 129 units.
Check at 150 units: 150 x $28 - $3,600 = $4,200 - $3,600 = $600 profit. Good.

Now the hire kicks in at unit 151: fixed costs become $4,500.
At 151 units: 151 x $28 - $4,500 = $4,228 - $4,500 = -$272. A loss.
Second break-even: $4,500 / $28 = 160.7, so 161 units.

So you are profitable from 129 to 150 units, dip back into loss from 151 to 160, and turn profitable again at 161. Step costs create that valley. If demand sits near 155, the smart move may be turning work away or raising price — growing from 150 to 155 units literally loses money.
A job offers $27.50 an hour, full-time. What is that as an annual salary?

Full-time is 40 hours a week x 52 weeks = 2,080 hours.

$27.50 x 2,080 = $57,200 a year.

Quick mental version worth memorizing: hourly wage x 2,000 is a fast estimate ($55,000 here), then adjust up 4% for the exact figure. The conversion runs the other way too when comparing a salary offer against contract work — but remember a salary usually carries benefits and paid time off that the hourly figure here does not, so $57,200 salaried and $57,200 of contract income are not the same money.
I am salaried at $68,000. My boss says that is 'about $32 an hour.' But I actually work 45-hour weeks. What is my real hourly rate?

On paper (40 hrs/week): 2,080 hours a year, so $68,000 / 2,080 = $32.69 an hour. Your boss's 'about $32' is fair for the nominal schedule.

At your actual 45-hour weeks: 45 x 52 = 2,340 hours, so $68,000 / 2,340 = $29.06 an hour.

The 5 unpaid extra hours a week dilute your rate by about $3.63 an hour — roughly 260 extra hours a year for free. That is the number to bring to a raise conversation: not 'I work hard,' but 'my effective rate is $29.06 against a $32.69 nominal rate.'
A recipe serves 6 and uses 450 g flour, 180 g sugar, and 3 eggs. I need to serve 15. Scale it.

Scale factor: 15 / 6 = 2.5.

Flour: 450 x 2.5 = 1,125 g.
Sugar: 180 x 2.5 = 450 g.
Eggs: 3 x 2.5 = 7.5 eggs.

Everything scales by the same factor — that is the whole method. The eggs expose the practical limit: you cannot crack half an egg easily, so use 7 large eggs plus a splash of milk, or 8 and accept a slightly richer result. Ingredients by weight scale exactly; ingredients by count round to what the kitchen allows.
My sauce recipe makes 3.2 liters and calls for 24 g salt, 2.4 L stock, and 800 ml cream. I only need 800 ml of sauce. Scale everything down.

Scale factor: 800 ml / 3,200 ml = 0.25 — a clean quarter batch.

Salt: 24 x 0.25 = 6 g.
Stock: 2.4 L x 0.25 = 0.6 L, so 600 ml.
Cream: 800 x 0.25 = 200 ml.

One caution with the salt: seasoning does not always scale perfectly linearly in practice — smaller volumes can taste saltier at the same ratio because there is less margin for evaporation differences. Make it with the 6 g, taste, and adjust. The arithmetic gives you the starting point; your palate signs off.
The exchange rate is 1 euro = 1.08 US dollars. I have $250. How many euros do I get, ignoring fees?

You are converting dollars into euros, so divide by the rate:

$250 / 1.08 = EUR 231.48 (rounded to cents).

Inverse check: EUR 231.48 x 1.08 = $249.9984, which rounds back to $250.00 — the one-cent wobble is just rounding at the cent level.

The direction is where people slip: '1 euro = 1.08 dollars' means euros are the more valuable unit, so $250 must buy FEWER than 250 euros. If your conversion ever produces a bigger number in the stronger currency, you multiplied when you should have divided.
A client in London owes me 640 pounds. The rate is $1.27 per pound, but the transfer service keeps 1.5%. How many dollars actually land in my account?

Convert first: GBP 640 x $1.27 = $812.80.
Fee: 1.5% of $812.80 = $12.19.
You receive: $812.80 x 0.985 = $800.61 (rounded to cents).

So the 1.5% fee costs you $12.19 on this invoice. Worth knowing for pricing: to net the full $812.80 after a 1.5% fee, you would have to bill $812.80 / 0.985 = $825.18 worth — about GBP 650. Fees quoted as small percents are still real money on every single invoice, all year.
A contractor charges $520 a day and works 4-day weeks. What is that as an average monthly income?

Annualize first, then divide by 12:

Weekly: $520 x 4 = $2,080.
Annual: $2,080 x 52 = $108,160.
Monthly average: $108,160 / 12 = $9,013.33.

Note why you cannot just do $2,080 x 4 = $8,320: a month is not 4 weeks, it is 52/12 = 4.33 weeks on average. The naive version understates income by about $693 a month — enough to wreck a budget or a tax estimate. Any weekly figure converts to monthly through the year, never through 4.
A delivery run is 240 miles. At 60 mph versus 70 mph, how much time do I actually save, and what is it worth if my time is $30 an hour?

At 60 mph: 240 / 60 = 4.00 hours.
At 70 mph: 240 / 70 = 3.43 hours.
Saved: 0.5714 hours, which is 34.3 minutes.
Value: 0.5714 x $30 = $17.14.

So the faster pace buys you about half an hour for about $17 of time value — before counting the extra fuel (cars burn noticeably more per mile at 70 than 60) and the risk. Speed feels dramatic from the driver's seat; over a fixed distance, the arithmetic is always this modest, because time saved shrinks as speed grows.
I am painting a room 12 by 15 feet with 9-foot ceilings. A gallon covers 350 square feet and costs $42.99. How much paint and money for the walls, one coat?

Wall area: two walls of 12 x 9 = 108 sq ft each, and two of 15 x 9 = 135 sq ft each.
Total: 2 x 108 + 2 x 135 = 216 + 270 = 486 sq ft. (Ceiling not included.)

Gallons needed: 486 / 350 = 1.39 gallons.
Paint is sold in whole gallons, so you buy 2: 2 x $42.99 = $85.98.

You will have about 0.6 of a gallon left — fine for touch-ups. Two coats would need 972 sq ft of coverage, i.e., 2.78 gallons, so 3 gallons at $128.97. Always compute coverage for the number of coats you actually plan; 'one gallon covers 350' means per coat.
Road trip: 312 miles, my car gets 28 mpg, gas is $3.59 a gallon. What does the drive cost in fuel?

Gallons used: 312 / 28 = 11.14 gallons.
Fuel cost: 11.14 x $3.59 = $40.00 (rounded to cents).

Almost exactly forty dollars — a coincidence of these particular numbers, but a memorable benchmark: at roughly $3.60 gas and high-20s mpg, highway miles cost about 13 cents each in fuel. Budget the round trip at $80 and you will not be surprised.
A software subscription is $13.99 a month or $119.99 a year paid upfront. How much does the annual plan save?

Monthly plan over a year: $13.99 x 12 = $167.88.
Annual plan: $119.99.
Saving: $167.88 - $119.99 = $47.89 a year, which is 28.5% less.

That is a strong discount — equivalent to getting about 3.4 months free. The catch is commitment: if there is a real chance you cancel within the first 8 or 9 months, the monthly plan can still win, because $119.99 / $13.99 = 8.6 months is the break-even point. Pay annually only for tools you are confident will survive 9 months of use.
I earn $24 an hour. Last week I worked 46 hours with overtime at time-and-a-half after 40. What was my gross pay?

Regular hours: 40 x $24 = $960.
Overtime rate: $24 x 1.5 = $36 an hour.
Overtime hours: 46 - 40 = 6, so 6 x $36 = $216.
Gross: $960 + $216 = $1,176.00.

Check the structure: the 6 extra hours are worth 9 straight-time hours (6 x 1.5), so the week paid like 49 hours at base rate: 49 x $24 = $1,176. Matches. If you worked that schedule every week it would annualize to $1,176 x 52 = $61,152 — but overtime is rarely that reliable, so budget on the $960 base and treat the rest as windfall.
My two product lines have margins of 10% and 30%. My bookkeeper averaged them and reported a 20% overall margin. Revenue was $900,000 on the first line and $100,000 on the second. Is 20% right?

It is not — the true blended margin is 12%.

Profit, line 1: $900,000 x 10% = $90,000.
Profit, line 2: $100,000 x 30% = $30,000.
Total profit: $120,000 on $1,000,000 revenue = 12%.

Averaging the percents (10 + 30) / 2 = 20% pretends the two lines are equal in size. They are not: the 10% line is 90% of the business, so the blend sits close to 10%. Percentages can only be averaged when their bases are equal; otherwise weight them by the base — here, by revenue. This error flatters any business whose big line is its weak one, which is exactly when accuracy matters most.
A store offers 30% off, then an extra 20% off the sale price at checkout. My friend says that is 50% off total. Settle it.

Your friend is wrong: it is 44% off, not 50%.

On a $100 item:
After 30% off: $100 x 0.70 = $70.
After the extra 20% off: $70 x 0.80 = $56.
Total discount: $100 - $56 = $44, which is 44%.

Successive percents multiply, they do not add, because the second discount applies to the already-reduced price — 20% of $70 is $14, not $20. 'Add the percents' overstates every stacked discount. The one-line version: final price factor = 0.7 x 0.8 = 0.56.

I already paid $1,200 nonrefundable for a training program. Finishing it costs $300 more in materials. A different program costs $650 all-in and is slightly better for my goals. My gut says I cannot waste the $1,200. What does the arithmetic say?

The $1,200 is gone in both futures — spent, nonrefundable, identical either way. It cannot be part of the comparison, because a cost that does not change between options cannot favor one of them.

Compare only what each path costs from today:
Finish the current program: $300 more.
Switch: $650 more.

On cost alone, finishing is $350 cheaper from here. The switch is justified only if 'slightly better for my goals' is worth more than $350 to you — a real question, but a values question, not an arithmetic one.

The $1,200 argues emotionally because it feels like waste. But paying $650 to honor $1,200 you cannot recover is how sunk costs collect rent. Decide on the $300 versus $650, and let the $1,200 be a lesson already paid for.
I buy supplies from two vendors. I spend $60 at Vendor A at $4 per unit, and $60 at Vendor B at $6 per unit. My average cost per unit is obviously $5, right?

It feels obvious and it is wrong.

Units from A: $60 / $4 = 15 units.
Units from B: $60 / $6 = 10 units.
Total: $120 spent for 25 units.
Average cost: $120 / 25 = $4.80 per unit.

Averaging $4 and $6 gives $5.00 only if you bought equal NUMBERS of units. You bought equal DOLLARS, which means more units at the cheaper price, dragging the true average below $5. Equal quantities -> simple average. Equal spending -> total money divided by total units. Mixing the two up overstates your costs here by 20 cents a unit.
A lender quotes a $4,000 loan for 2 years at '8% flat.' My credit union offers 8% APR amortizing. Flat sounds simpler — is it the same cost?

arguments.code:
P, n = 4000, 24
r = 0.08 / 12
pmt = P * r / (1 - (1 + r) ** -n)
print('amortizing interest:', round(pmt * n - P, 2))
print('flat interest:', P * 0.08 * 2)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
amortizing interest: 341.82
flat interest: 640.0

Not the same cost — not close.

Flat 8%: interest is charged on the ORIGINAL $4,000 for the whole term: $4,000 x 8% x 2 = $640.00.
Amortizing 8% APR: interest totals $341.82.

The flat loan costs $298.18 more — nearly double — at the same headline '8%.' The trick: with an amortizing loan your balance shrinks monthly, so interest is charged on less and less. Flat interest charges you for money you have already paid back. In effective-APR terms the flat loan behaves like roughly a 15% amortizing loan.

Any time a rate is quoted as 'flat,' 'add-on,' or per-month on the original amount, convert before you compare. Headline rates are only comparable when the balance basis is the same.
The bigger bottle must be the better deal: 64 oz of detergent for $6.40, or the family-size 96 oz for $10.08. Family size wins, right?

Check the unit price before trusting the shelf placement:

64 oz: $6.40 / 64 = exactly 10.0 cents per oz.
96 oz: $10.08 / 96 = 10.5 cents per oz.

The family size is MORE expensive per ounce — you pay a $0.48 premium over buying the same 96 oz as smaller bottles ($9.60 worth at the small-bottle rate). 'Family size,' 'value pack,' and 'club size' are packaging claims, not price claims; stores know shoppers assume bigger is cheaper and occasionally price against the assumption. The unit-price shelf tag exists precisely for this. Ten seconds of division beats the packaging every time.
A store will rent me a washer for $65 a month on a 24-month rent-to-own deal, or sell me the same washer for $899. What does renting really cost, and when does buying pull ahead?

Total rent-to-own cost: $65 x 24 = $1,560.
Purchase price: $899.
Premium for renting: $1,560 - $899 = $661 — you pay 74% more for the same machine.

Break-even: $899 / $65 = 13.8 months. If you would keep the washer past about 14 months, buying is cheaper, and by month 24 you are $661 ahead.

Rent-to-own is really a loan with the interest hidden in the monthly price — on these numbers it works out to a very expensive one. It can still make sense if you genuinely need the machine for under a year, or cannot access any other credit. But call it what it is: financing, priced at $661.
Two mortgage quotes on $200,000 for 30 years: 6.25% versus 6.75%. Half a percentage point sounds like nothing. What is it actually worth per month?

At 6.25%: $1,231.43 a month.
At 6.75%: $1,297.20 a month.
Difference: $65.76 a month.

Half a percentage point is $65.76 every month — $789.12 a year, and about $23,674 over the full 30 years if you never refinance.

'Percentage point' language makes rate gaps sound tiny because the unit is small. Always translate a rate difference into dollars on YOUR loan amount and term before deciding it does not matter. On a mortgage, half a point is a car payment's worth of money spread over the loan's life.
My investment went up 50% last year and down 50% this year. Average return zero, so I should be even. My statement disagrees. Why?

Your statement is right. Run $4,000 through it:

Up 50%: $4,000 x 1.50 = $6,000.
Down 50%: $6,000 x 0.50 = $3,000.

You are at $3,000 — down 25% overall, not even.

The arithmetic mean of +50% and -50% is 0%, but returns do not add; they multiply: 1.50 x 0.50 = 0.75. The correct 'average' for growth is the geometric mean: sqrt(0.75) = 0.866, i.e., -13.4% per year.

The asymmetry is fundamental: a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to undo it. Any pitch that averages yearly percents with simple addition is quietly flattering the results — insist on the multiplied (geometric) figure.
An ad screams 'SAVE 200%!' and another store has 'buy one, get one 50% off' on $40 shirts. What is each offer really worth?

The 200% claim is impossible on its face: saving 100% would mean the item is free. 'Save 200%' is either nonsense or it means something else entirely, like comparing against a competitor's price twice as high. A discount cannot exceed 100% of the price you pay.

Buy one, get one 50% off: two $40 shirts cost $40 + $20 = $60 instead of $80. Total saving: $20 / $80 = 25% off the pair.

BOGO-half is a 25% discount wearing a 50% costume — the full-price shirt carries the deal. It is still a fair offer if you wanted two shirts; it is a trap if it talks you into a second shirt you did not want, because then you spent $60 to 'save' $20.
